words.title: dhamma (verses 1–2, 20)
words.statement: One Indic word with many senses: what bears or upholds, the nature of things, states of mind, the teaching.
words.decided: Translate by context, not with one fixed word. In verses 1–2 the context is lived experience: the verse sets up the wheel following the ox. (Owner, 2026-11-09)

words.title: vera: “hostility”
words.statement: Enmity held against someone (verses 3–5). Options were enmity, hostility, hatred.
words.decided: “Hostility” (B). “Hatred” is kept for dosa; “enmity” is less well understood; the Chinese “resentment” is interesting but sits with the one receiving hostility. Condition: base, plural and negation must read as an intelligible set in English (see verse 5). (Owner, 2026-11-09)

words.title: The stained robe (verses 9–10)
words.statement: The Pāli puns on kasāva, stain, and kāsāva, the dyed ochre robe.
words.decided: Keep the pun (A). “Impurities” sat oddly after verse 7–8's warning about attractiveness; stain/robe avoids that. (Owner, 2026-11-09)

words.title: sanantano: “age-old”, not “eternal” (verse 5)
words.statement: Sanantano means from of old, perpetual. Neither the Chinese nor the Tibetan says eternal.

words.title: dhamma as the teaching (verse 20)
words.statement: Where dhamma clearly means the Buddha's teaching: plain English, or the word itself.

words.title: Māra, across the book
words.statement: Māra recurs through the Dhammapada, sometimes as a figure (his realm, his army, his flower-tipped arrows), sometimes as a force, as in verses 7–8. This sets the default; a verse can still depart (see 7.5).

options.text: Keep the name “Māra”, explained once on the home page.
“the Tempter”: personified and self-explaining, and works wherever Māra is a figure.
Render by context each time (temptation, death, the Tempter).

words.title: samaṇa: “renunciant”, not “recluse” (verses 19–20)
words.statement: A samaṇa is someone who has left household life to seek liberation by spiritual striving; the Buddha's monks were samaṇas, as were other wanderers. “Recluse” suggests a hermit; “mendicant” is already our word for bhikkhu, the begging monk; “renunciant” names what the samaṇa has done.

words.title: Other recurring words
words.statement: Words every tradition agrees on but with several possible English renderings. Approve as a block or name the ones to change.

principles.title: Count traditions by family
principles.statement: The Tibetan translates the Sanskrit Udānavarga, so the two count as one voice. Where the Tibetan alone departs from its Sanskrit (verse 1's “head cut off by a wheel”), that is a translation matter.

principles.title: A lone reading starts as the outsider
principles.statement: A reading found in one tradition only does not go into the first draft. It can still be chosen on its merits, as the best reading; the choice is then marked as such.

principles.title: The Chinese is a reading too
principles.statement: Where the Chinese says the same thing in its own idiom, it counts as agreement. Where it has its own image, the image is a candidate for the best reading (verse 2's “shadow following the body”), never thrown out by default.

principles.title: Keep every Pāli line
principles.statement: Partial parallels inform but never add or remove lines. Where other traditions lack a line, that is noted, not treated as evidence against it.

principles.title: Family against family: decide verse by verse
principles.statement: When Pāli and Patna stand against Gāndhārī, Sanskrit and Tibetan, the evidence is roughly even, so it is a question for you in that verse.

principles.title: Same idea, different word
principles.statement: The first draft uses the word with the widest support, the Pāli's on a tie. You may prefer another tradition's image when it is better.
